planting.note: Divide or pot up rooted cuttings year-round indoors, or move outdoors to a shaded, humid spot after the last frost; Frankie is a compact fittonia with olive-green leaves overlaid in fine rose-pink veining.

directions: Grow in constantly moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light or deep outdoor shade with high humidity; fittonias wilt dramatically when they dry out but usually recover with a thorough watering. Frankie forms a low, spreading mat of small olive-green leaves densely netted with rose-pink veins, staying more compact than the species and suiting terrariums, dish gardens, and shaded ground cover in frost-free climates. It rarely flowers indoors and is grown entirely for foliage; pinch trailing stems to keep the mat dense and propagate easily from stem cuttings kept warm and humid until rooted.

common_name: Ruby Red Fittonia (Deep Red-Veined Nerve Plant)

planting.note: Divide or pot up rooted cuttings year-round indoors, or set outdoors in deep, humid shade after the last frost; Ruby Red is a fittonia with dark green leaves saturated in deep red-purple veining.

directions: Grow in constantly moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light or deep outdoor shade with high humidity, since low humidity causes crisp brown leaf edges. Ruby Red carries the boldest coloring of the common fittonia selections, with nearly solid deep red-purple veins covering dark green leaf blades, giving a much richer effect than the pink- or white-veined types. It stays low and mounding, making it a strong accent color in mixed terrariums or shaded container plantings; trim leggy stems back hard to renew density and root the cuttings for more plants.

planting.note: Divide or pot up rooted cuttings year-round indoors, or move outdoors to deep, humid shade after the last frost; Josan is a larger-leaved fittonia with prominent ivory-white veining over medium green leaves.

directions: Grow in constantly moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light or deep outdoor shade with steady humidity; Josan's larger leaves make it more forgiving of brief lapses in humidity than the miniature fittonia cultivars. Medium green, quilted leaves are traced in bold ivory-white veins in a coarser, more open pattern than compact selections, giving a leafier look better suited to hanging baskets and mixed foliage bowls than tight terrariums. Pinch growing tips regularly to prevent legginess and keep the mound full, and propagate new plants from stem cuttings rooted in warm, humid conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Komodo Dragon is one of the largest hostas available, needing several seasons and ample room to reach full size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade with room to spread, since Komodo Dragon can eventually form a mound wider than most garden beds allow for a single specimen. Enormous, heavily corrugated, dark olive-green leaves rise on thick petioles to form one of the largest hostas in cultivation, used as a bold specimen or anchor plant rather than a mass-planted ground cover. Like other giant sieboldiana-type hostas it is slow to reach mature size, often taking four or more years, and rewards deep, fertile soil and consistent moisture with correspondingly larger leaves each season. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on stout scapes held just above the foliage in summer.

common_name: Devon Green Hosta (Glossy Ruffled Dark Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Devon Green forms a low, dense mound of glossy, deeply rippled dark green leaves and holds its color well through the season.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Devon Green tolerates somewhat drier soil and more morning light than many hostas once established, without losing its glossy sheen. Small, deeply wavy, high-gloss dark green leaves form a tidy, low mound that holds its shape and color from spring through fall better than most green-leaved hostas, resisting the fading some cultivars show in summer heat. Its compact, well-behaved habit and shiny foliage make it a reliable edging or front-of-border plant that pairs well with variegated or blue-leaved neighbors; lavender flowers appear on modest scapes in mid to late summer.
